item.title: U.S. CISA adds IBM, SignalWire FreeSwitch, OpenSSH, and GPUStack flaws to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog
item.description:
U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) adds IBM, SignalWire FreeSwitch, OpenSSH, and GPUStack flaws to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog.

The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added IBM, SignalWire FreeSwitch, OpenSSH, and GPUStack vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog:

Below are the flaws added to the catalog:

  • CVE-2026-102895 GPUStack Improper Authentication Vulnerability 
  • CVE-2026-116779 SignalWire FreeSwitch Code Injection Vulnerability 
  • CVE-2026-123158 OpenBSD OpenSSH Unexpected Status Code or Return Value Vulnerability 
  • CVE-2026-123218 IBM Aspera Faspex Incorrect Authorization Vulnerability 

The first issue added to the catalog, CVE-2026-102895 (CVSS score of 9.8), is an improper authentication vulnerability affecting GPUStack, an open-source platform used to manage GPU clusters and AI model deployments. The flaw allows remote, unauthenticated attackers to bypass authentication and obtain administrator privileges by making requests appear to originate from the local system. Successful exploitation can expose sensitive information, create persistent administrator API keys, modify configurations and potentially execute arbitrary code. Exploitation has been observed in the wild against a GPUStack 2.1.1 deployment. Security researcher Javier Sixto reported the in-the-wild exploitation, but no specific threat group has been identified. The issue affects versions before 2.2.0.

The second issue, CVE-2026-116779 (CVSS score of 9.8), is a code injection vulnerability in SignalWire FreeSWITCH, an open-source communications platform. The flaw allows attackers to send specially crafted SIP MESSAGE requests and abuse the API chat protocol to execute FreeSWITCH API commands. Depending on the configuration, this can expose credentials and configuration data, manipulate telephone calls and execute operating system commands with the privileges of the FreeSWITCH process. SignalWire confirmed that exploitation has been observed in the wild. The vulnerability was added to CISA’s KEV catalog on November 9, 2026, but no information identifying the attackers or a specific campaign has been disclosed. FreeSWITCH versions before 1.11.3 are affected.

The third issue, CVE-2026-123158 (CVSS score of 8.1), is an authentication bypass vulnerability affecting OpenSSH. Under specific conditions, when OpenSSH runs on Linux systems using the musl C library without Pluggable Authentication Modules (PAM), the SSH server may incorrectly interpret password input as a password hash. A remote, unauthenticated attacker can exploit the flaw by submitting a specially crafted password to bypass authentication and access affected accounts. CISA added the vulnerability to its KEV catalog on November 6, 2026, indicating that exploitation has been observed. However, no specific threat actor or attack campaign has been publicly identified. OpenSSH versions before 10.6p2 are affected.

The fourth issue, CVE-2026-123218 (CVSS score of 9.8), is an incorrect authorization vulnerability affecting IBM Aspera Faspex 5. It allows an authenticated user to craft a specific message that bypasses authorization checks and potentially gain full administrative privileges. Successful exploitation could give attackers access to sensitive information and allow them to modify or disrupt the affected system. IBM disclosed the vulnerability on November 7, 2026, and released a fix in Aspera Faspex 5.0.19 PL1. I found no public confirmation of exploitation in the wild or information identifying attackers at the time of writing. Versions 5.0.0 through 5.0.19 are affected.

According to Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 22-01: Reducing the Significant Risk of Known Exploited Vulnerabilities, FCEB agencies have to address the identified vulnerabilities by the due date to protect their networks against attacks exploiting the flaws in the catalog.

Experts also recommend that private organizations review the Catalog and address the vulnerabilities in their infrastructure.

CISA orders federal agencies to fix the two vulnerabilities by November 12, 2026.

item.title: Microsoft November Patch Tuesday: one exploited Outlook bug and 30 wormable flaws
item.description:
Microsoft November Patch Tuesday security updates fix 1,090 flaws, including one exploited Outlook bug and 30 potentially wormable issues.

Microsoft November Patch Tuesday addressed about 1,090 new vulnerabilities, which is less than the roughly 1,400 last month. Two months in a row now exceed every previous year from Microsoft, and the overall count is a bit confusing, so other trackers report different totals.

The release covers Windows and its components, Office, networking and remote access, graphics, media and printing, storage and file systems, .NET and Visual Studio, security and identity, Azure and cloud, Exchange Server, Dynamics and Xbox. Only one bug is under active attack and none is publicly known. ZDI says that doesn’t mean less exploitation, only fewer zero-days, and it guesses that AI is better at reversing patches than at finding and exploiting bugs in closed-source software.

The exploited bug is CVE-2026-124194, an Outlook spoofing flaw, and its name undersells the impact. An attacker sends a crafted message file and talks the user into opening it, and Outlook connects to an attacker-controlled location without the usual external-content warning, which leaks the user’s NTLMv2 hash.

“An unauthenticated attacker could send a specially crafted message file and convince a user to open it in an affected version of Microsoft Outlook. Opening the file could cause Outlook to connect to an attacker-controlled network location without displaying the usual external-content warning, potentially disclosing authentication information that could be used to impersonate the user. Exploitation requires network connectivity and user interaction.” reads the advisory. “An attacker must send a user a malicious Office file and convince them to open it.”

The attacker can then authenticate as that user. The Preview Pane isn’t an attack path and the CVSS score is only 6.5, but ZDI says to put it first because Microsoft marks it as exploited.

CVE-2026-116928 is a Windows Search remote code execution bug reached through Exchange Server. An unauthenticated attacker emails a crafted attachment, and the bug triggers when the server indexes it automatically, so the recipient never opens anything. It’s zero-click, scores CVSS 9.8, and ZDI rates it more severe than any of the nine patches Exchange gets this month.

CVE-2026-119958 hits the Windows LDAP service. An unauthenticated attacker sends crafted LDAP calls over the network, triggers an out-of-bounds write and runs code in the service context, which could be destructive on domain controllers. ZDI says to test and deploy it quickly. CVE-2026-119952, a Schannel remote code execution flaw, is marked “Exploitation More Likely”, one of only a few Critical patches with that rating, and its high attack complexity is why the score is lower.

CVE-2026-119990, an Azure OpenAI elevation of privilege bug, got a bulletin that said “Customer Action Required: Yes” and then listed nothing to do. An unauthenticated attacker could send a crafted request over the internet and reach orchestration information, change workflows or disrupt the service. Microsoft has since revised it to say no customer action is needed. A bulletin that says action required and lists none is the most relaxed urgent notice you’ll read this month.

Two more stand out for their components. CVE-2026-95962 is a use-after-free in the little-documented Windows Virtual Filtering Platform, reachable with a crafted network packet and needing no authentication or user interaction. It involves a race condition, but ZDI notes those get beaten all the time at Pwn2Own. CVE-2026-112967 is a heap overflow in the Xbox Live Networking Service with a CVSS of 9.8, and ZDI doesn’t think exploitation is likely but enjoys imagining Xbox Live exploits in the wild.

ZDI counts 30 wormable bugs this month, down from 59 last month. Seventeen carry advisory wording about an unauthenticated attacker running code over the network with no interaction, and 13 use variant wording or have no FAQ but show the same pattern in their summaries and CVSS vectors. ZDI warns it may be wrong on some, since a few advisories are light on detail.

Network-facing services like DNS, DHCP, LDAP and Exchange deserve the earliest attention.

“I may be wrong about some of these, since a few advisories are light on detail.” concludes ZDI. “As always, I recommend testing and deploying these patches quickly, especially for network-facing services like DNS, DHCP, LDAP, and Exchange”

Pierluigi Paganini

(SecurityAffairs – hacking, Patch Tuesday)

item.title: Hackers Advertise a $1,000 Gmail Tool That Allegedly Survives Password Resets
item.description:
Hackers advertise a $1,000-a-month tool claiming persistent Gmail access after password resets, but its effectiveness remains unverified.

A developer of hacking tools is selling a $1,000 per month feature that allegedly gives criminals continuous access to Gmail inboxes. The cybersecurity firm Hudson Rock reports that the tool can keep reading a victim’s mailbox after a password change, after the browser closes and after sessions are revoked.

“Remus Stealer is advertising a way for criminals to open a compromised Gmail inbox directly from a stolen-device record.” reads the report published by cybersecurity firm Hudson Rock. “Its latest pitch goes further: the operator claims access continues even after the victim changes their password or revokes sessions.”

The tool belongs to Remus Stealer, an infostealer, meaning malware that steals data from infected computers. Remus supposedly gives its operators a searchable inbox right inside a stolen-device dashboard. Hudson Rock says it spoke with the developer and with a customer who used it, and the customer supplied screenshots of messages, timestamps and a control for sharing a mailbox with other operators.

If the claims are true, the risk goes beyond a single Gmail inbox. Attackers could read password reset links and verification codes, allowing them to access other accounts linked to that email address. This makes Gmail a valuable target because many online services use it to recover accounts.

“In the supplied , Remus promotes email-code interception without collecting browser cookie files, claims that password changes and session revocation do not stop it, and advertises shareable mailbox links. The feature is listed as Enterprise-only; the advertises that tier at $1,000 per month.” continues the report. “The sharing claim concerns giving other operators access to an already acquired mailbox through the service. The material does not show a victim being infected by opening one of those links.”

It is still unclear how the tool works. Hudson Rock says Remus does not steal browser cookies, while its developer claims that changing the Gmail password does not stop access. The developer has not shared technical details. He only said that the malware interacts with browser memory, but this does not explain how it can maintain access after a password change or when active sessions are revoked.

Hudson Rock believes Remus may obtain or create an authorization token while the victim is logged into Gmail through a browser. A remote component could then use this authorization to access emails even after the malware has stopped running, as long as Google continues to accept it. Tom’s Guide also reports that the tool can bypass Google’s anti-fraud checks and says it has contacted Google for comment.

However, other reports highlight some important uncertainties. CyberInsider says Hudson Rock has not confirmed that the tool can maintain access after a password change, nor has it established that the feature exploits a Gmail vulnerability. Hudson Rock has not conducted a controlled test to show that Remus can still access newly received emails after the victim changes their password and revokes existing sessions and third-party access. According to Cybernews, the developer describes the feature as a Gmail “zero-day”. However, this claim has not been independently reproduced.

The business side is more concrete. CyberInsider says the mailbox feature sits in an Enterprise tier at $1,000 per month, with shareable mailbox links so criminals can hand an inbox they’ve already compromised to others. The actor behind Remus Stealer offers the MaaS with three subscription tiers: Basic at $250, Pro at $500 and Enterprise at $1,000.

This kind of claim has a history. In late 2023, a developer called PRISMA surfaced an exploit that regenerated persistent Google cookies by manipulating a token and account ID pair, and Lumma then used it so access continued after a password reset. It’s a precedent and not proof, since Remus’ mechanism is unknown, and Hudson Rock still treats a Google password change as an essential recovery step, while saying victims should also look for other ways an attacker could keep access.

The tool is marketed to “enterprise” customers, so most users are unlikely to be targeted. It will probably be used mainly against organizations and high-profile individuals. Hudson Rock recommends that victims first disconnect and clean the infected computer before accessing their trusted accounts again. They should then change compromised passwords using a clean device and review their signed-in devices to remove suspicious sessions and third-party access.

Hudson Rock also advises users to check Gmail settings for unauthorized changes and secure any other accounts that use the compromised mailbox for password resets or verification codes. Other basic precautions remain important: watch out for phishing emails with urgent messages, spelling mistakes or suspicious sender addresses, and keep antivirus software up to date. Tom’s Guide expects Google to introduce additional Gmail protections if the tool proves as effective as its developer claims.

For now, this is a vendor’s marketing claim supported by customer screenshots and Hudson Rock’s investigation, not a confirmed Gmail vulnerability. One important detail offers some reassurance: attackers must first infect the victim’s computer and compromise their mailbox before they can use the tool.

“Remus is marketing an integrated mailbox-reading capability, and a customer has endorsed its claimed persistence. The most plausible broad model is reuse of access obtained or established during endpoint compromise.” concludes the report. “The evidence does not identify the mechanism or show fresh mail remaining accessible after comprehensive recovery.”

Pierluigi Paganini

(SecurityAffairs – hacking, Gmail)

item.title: WhiteArmor Demands $5 Million from Maersk, Claims Theft of 100GB of Data
item.description:
Maersk confirms a data breach involving a legacy system, while WhiteArmor claims 100GB of stolen data and demands a $5 million ransom.

A.P. Moller Maersk, the Danish shipping giant, says it identified an IT security incident involving unauthorized access and data extraction from one of its local legacy systems, one inherited from a previous acquisition.

“Maersk has identified an IT security incident involving unauthorised access and data extraction from one of our local legacy systems from a previous acquisition.” reads the statement published by Maersk on November 11. “Our findings so far strongly suggest no sensitive data has been disclosed. The incident is isolated to a local system, and we have found no indication that there has been any impact on other Maersk systems or customer and partner systems that connect to Maersk through integrations such as APIs and EDI.”

According to Maersk, its cyber security team started a full investigation as soon as it found the problem, and it’s still going. The company says swift action secured the affected system. Its findings so far strongly suggest no sensitive data has been disclosed, and it says the incident is isolated to that one local system.

Maersk has found no sign that other Maersk systems were affected, or the customer and partner systems that connect to it through integrations such as APIs and EDI. It doesn’t expect disruption for customers, who can book and manage shipments as usual. It promises updates and says it will inform any affected parties if it finds a need to.

Maersk didn’t name the system, the type of data or the date of the intrusion. However, the cybercrime group WhiteArmor added the company to its Tor data leak site:

WhiteArmor demanded a $5 million ransom in Bitcoin, giving Maersk 30 days to pay. The group claims to have stolen about 100 GB of data from the OCF/LF Logistics platform, which supports logistics and supply chain operations.

“”Your contract-logistics arm, the former LF Logistics, runs fulfilment for many of the world’s largest consumer brands,” states the leak site. “Five million dollars is roughly four hours of that EBITDA.””

Maersk acquired LF Logistics, the company that developed the platform, from the Li & Fung Group in 2022. This could match Maersk’s reference to an old system inherited through an acquisition, although the company has not confirmed this connection.

According to the attackers, the stolen data includes nearly 30,000 driver records, passwords stored in plain text, 33 super admin accounts and signed delivery receipts. The group also claims to have stolen inventory records, purchase orders, advance shipping notices and 27,842 mobile device logs containing phone numbers, email addresses and IMEI numbers. These details come from the attackers and have not been independently verified. Maersk’s statement does not confirm their claims. WhiteArmor also tried to justify its demand, saying the $5 million ransom represents roughly four hours of revenue for the logistics business.

“We do not anticipate disruption to operations for customers at this time, and customers can continue to use Maersk platforms to book and manage their shipments as usual.” concludes the statement. “We will keep customers updated as more relevant information becomes available, and if we identify any need to inform impacted parties of any further findings, we will do so.”

The scale of Maersk’s operations explains why this incident matters. A.P. Moller-Maersk is one of the world’s largest integrated shipping and logistics companies, playing a major role in global trade and supply chains. It operates around 700 container ships, representing approximately 13.5% of global container fleet capacity, and manages 60 terminals across 35 countries. The company employs about 100,000 people in 130 countries and provides services covering ocean shipping, port operations, warehousing, customs clearance and end-to-end supply chain management.

Maersk reported approximately $54 billion in revenue and $2.9 billion in net profit in 2025. Its global reach and reliance on interconnected IT systems make cybersecurity a major concern. A breach involving even an older, locally operated platform could expose sensitive business and personal information, including data belonging to drivers, customers and logistics partners, even if the company’s main systems remain unaffected.

In 2017, NotPetya forced the company to reinstall more than 4,000 servers and 45,000 workstations from scratch. It operated without IT for ten days and took damages of up to $300 million.

item.title: AI Pentest Tool AntiFox Abused To Steal AWS Credentials
item.description:
Arctic Wolf saw attackers use the AntiFox pentest platform to hit IIS servers and AWS accounts.

Arctic Wolf Labs has published research on attackers using AntiFox, an open-source, Chinese-language agentic penetration testing platform. These frameworks chain attack steps together with little human effort. In several intrusions, Alibaba Cloud systems hosting AntiFox interfaces were tied to confirmed attacks on internet-facing web services and the AWS environments behind them.

Two entry points showed up. In some cases, the attackers got into a public IIS application, though Arctic Wolf couldn’t identify the vulnerability. In others, they started with a valid AWS credential obtained by means nobody knows.

“Arctic Wolf is tracking the emerging use of self-hosted agentic penetration testing frameworks, including AntiFox, from public cloud infrastructure.” states the report published by Arctic Wolf, “In several recently observed intrusions, Alibaba Cloud systems hosting AntiFox interfaces were associated with confirmed malicious actions against internet-facing web services and associated AWS environments.”

The IIS attacks followed a similar pattern. The IIS worker process, w3wp.exe, created an ASPX web shell and then ran commands to gather information about the system. The attackers checked the user account, listed files in the application folder, reviewed file permissions using icacls and tested whether they could write files to the website’s main folder.

They then used PowerShell to read the web.config file, looking for database connection details and application settings. They also checked folders containing debug and error logs. Using credentials found in the configuration file, they tried to connect to an internal production database. Finally, they copied configuration files and logs into an upload folder that could be accessed through the website.

The AWS attacks moved quickly. AntiFox used valid IAM accounts and, in some cases, an assumed EC2 role. The attackers first checked their identity and permissions within AWS. They used commands such as GetCallerIdentity, GetUser, ListUsers, ListRoles, ListPolicies and ListKeys to discover available accounts, roles, policies and access keys. They also tried to obtain an authorization token for Amazon Elastic Container Registry (ECR).

In one intrusion, the source cycled through several AWS identities and sent hundreds of requests in about half an hour.

“The activity then rapidly enumerated services across the affected AWS environments, including IAM, EC2, S3, Lambda, Secrets Manager, KMS, RDS, ECS, EKS, Redshift, Athena, Glue, Systems Manager, API Gateway, CloudWatch, CloudFormation, DynamoDB, and Amazon Bedrock, using List, Get, and Describe operations.” continues the report. “After authorization failures, the activity continued across other services and concentrated on resources that remained accessible.”

Most requests came back as AccessDenied, but a few worked, and the attackers kept going where the doors were open.

Some sequences ended with a successful GetSecretValue request against a production secret. Others focused on S3, listing buckets, objects and versions, reading objects, then copying and deleting them. Nobody has to stay awake for that kind of persistence, which is the whole point of the tool.

Arctic Wolf’s concern is simple. These frameworks make penetration testing techniques easier to reach for attackers, and they make those techniques faster and more consistent in live attacks.

For hunting, start with AWS activity coming from hosting providers the identity has never used. Look for one IP address using many access keys, users or roles in a short time, and for fast runs of List, Get and Describe calls across unrelated services, especially from Boto3 or Botocore. Check GuardDuty for odd IAM user behavior, credential access, discovery and unusual calls from hosting networks.

On the Windows side, watch for w3wp.exe starting cmd.exe, powershell.exe, whoami.exe, icacls.exe or archive tools. Look for new .aspx files in upload, temporary and image-conversion folders, and for config or log files saved there under .txt or image extensions. PowerShell commands that read WebConfigurationManager, ConnectionStrings or AppSettings deserve a close look, and so does any AWS activity that starts soon after.

Organizations should enable AWS CloudTrail logging and monitor access to sensitive S3 storage. They should also use S3 versioning and Object Lock to protect important data from deletion. Alerts should flag suspicious access to stored secrets, especially when it follows unusual account activity.

Companies should identify all internet-facing applications and prioritize patching and protecting file upload, conversion and document-processing services. If an IIS process launches an unexpected command shell, administrators should isolate the server, preserve logs and forensic evidence, remove malicious files and change all exposed credentials.

They should also revoke compromised AWS sessions and access keys, enforce IMDSv2 and apply least-privilege permissions to limit what applications can access. As Arctic Wolf warns, a series of mostly denied requests does not mean the attack was unsuccessful.

item.title: Poland takes its national e-government platform offline after a cyberattack
item.description:
Poland takes its e-government platform ePUAP offline after stopping a cyberattack, disrupting access to public services.

Poland temporarily shut down ePUAP, the government platform citizens and businesses use to reach public services, after detecting and stopping a cyberattack. A notice on the government’s website says ePUAP electronic mailboxes are unavailable to citizens and public institutions.

ePUAP is a nationwide system for submitting official documents, communicating with government agencies and completing administrative procedures online. Digital Affairs Minister Krzysztof Gawkowski said on social media that the attack was detected and stopped.

“A cyberattack on the state-run ePUAP system has been detected and halted. The teams responsible for the system’s security took immediate action to maintain its stability, and technical work is currently underway to restore full functionality.” the Minister wrote on X. “The infrastructure of the Central IT Center remains secure.”

He added that security teams responded immediately and are working to restore full functionality.

The minister said the Central Information Technology Center, the agency responsible for ePUAP and other key digital services, was not affected. Officials explained that the platform was taken offline as a precaution, not because the attack caused any damage. Marek Gieorgica, a spokesperson for the Digital Affairs Ministry, told the Polish news agency PAP that the system had not been compromised or disrupted by the attack. In other words, the service was shut down even though no damage was reported.

Many details are still unknown. Authorities have not explained how the attack was carried out or who was behind it. There is also no public confirmation that attackers accessed government systems or stole sensitive data. The ministry has not provided a timeline for restoring services, saying they will return once security experts complete their checks.

The disruption could also briefly affect the Trusted Profile digital identity system, which lets people use public services and sign official documents electronically. For someone with a deadline for a filing, that’s a practical problem even if no data was lost.

The incident is part of a wider pattern. In recent months, Poland has faced several cyberattacks targeting government agencies, critical infrastructure and private companies. The Record reported that in October, Fakturownia, an online invoicing service, disclosed a data breach that may have exposed information belonging to its users, customers and business partners.

item.title: Zoom Fixes Critical Windows Vulnerability Allowing Privilege Escalation
item.description:
Zoom fixes two Windows Workplace flaws, including a critical bug that could let unauthenticated attackers remotely escalate privileges.

Zoom has released security updates to fix two vulnerabilities in Zoom Workplace for Windows. One is critical and could let attackers gain higher privileges on affected systems.

The vulnerabilities are:

  • CVE-2026-108186 (CVSS 9.6): An input validation flaw that could allow an attacker to gain higher privileges through a network connection, without logging in.
  • CVE-2026-108187 (CVSS 8.1): An origin validation flaw that could also allow an unauthenticated attacker to gain higher privileges remotely.

If successfully exploited, either vulnerability could allow attackers to increase their privileges without having an account or any special permissions on the affected system. Users should install the latest Zoom Workplace updates to protect their systems.

The first flaw was reported by the internal security team, while the second one was reported by the research shmoul.

CVE-2026-108187 affects Zoom Workplace for Windows releases earlier than 7.1.5, while CVE-2026-108186 impacts versions from 7.1.0 up to, but not including, 7.1.8.

The flaw can corrupt memory through a specially crafted message. Attackers could exploit it to target meeting participants, execute code without user interaction, steal data, activate cameras or microphones, and install malware.

In August, Zoom patched four vulnerabilities, including a critical zero-click flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-53413. CVE-2026-53413 is a memory corruption issue found by A Security that could allow a meeting participant to execute code on another participant’s computer.

Due to its impact, the researchers dubbed the flaw “Zoomsday,” it affects Zoom clients on all supported platforms and is linked to the proprietary protocol used by the annotation function. Zoom has now begun rolling out security updates to address the issue.

“Ⓐ Security, the Autonomous Offensive Security and Remediation Platform, discovered a critical flaw in Zoom that let an attacker take complete control of another user’s device during a live call. No click, no download, and nothing required of the victim but being in the meeting.” reads the report published by A Security. “The vulnerability is present in every version of Zoom on every device and operating system: Windows, Mac, iPhone, Android and Linux. The vulnerability exists in all versions up to and including 7.0.5.”

The flaw can corrupt memory through a specially crafted message. Attackers could exploit it to target meeting participants, execute code without user interaction, steal data, activate cameras or microphones, and install malware.

In July, Zoom fixed another critical Windows vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-53412 (CVSS score of 9.8), that could allow unauthenticated attackers to hijack user accounts. The flaw affects older versions of Workplace, the Windows VDI Client, and the Meeting SDK for Windows.

At this time, Zoom is not aware of attacks exploiting one of the above vulnerabilities. Users are recommended to apply the latest updates.

item.title: Predator, Pegasus and Graphite: Governments Accused of Spyware Abuse Face Little Accountability
item.description:
Europe’s spyware victims face years of legal battles and few answers as governments shield surveillance behind national security.

Greek journalist Thanasis Koukakis waited almost five years for a court to confirm what happened to him. His phone was infected with the infaous spyware Predator that gave whoever was watching access to his contacts, documents and messages, and even let them switch on his camera and microphone. IrpiMedia’s journalist and researcher Rosita Rijtano interviewed him and four other victims in a long investigation, and the picture it paints is bleak.

On February 26, a court in Athens convicted four executives linked to Intellexa, the company behind the Predator spyware. They include its founder, Tal Dilian, a former Israeli military intelligence commander. They face prison sentences of up to eight years for illegally accessing computer systems, violating data protection rules and breaking telecommunications privacy laws. Their sentences are suspended while they appeal, and investigators have not identified who ordered the surveillance. This is the first conviction of its kind in Europe, highlighting how rare such cases are.

The scandal began in 2021, when an international investigation led by Forbidden Stories revealed that dozens of European activists, politicians and journalists had been targeted with Pegasus spyware, developed by NSO Group. The company says it sells its products only to government intelligence and law enforcement agencies. Other spyware companies later came under scrutiny. In 2025, Citizen Lab found Italian phone numbers among those targeted by Paragon Solutions, an Israeli company that was later acquired by a US investment fund. Except in Greece, none of these cases has led to a criminal conviction.

“Yet, with the exception of Greece, none of these cases has resulted in a criminal conviction. In Spain and Hungary, victims say they have been unable even to obtain basic information about the surveillance they were subjected to, with authorities citing “national security.”” reads the report published by IrpiMedia.

In Spain and Hungary, victims say they can’t even get basic information about the surveillance, because authorities cite national security. Rebecca White, a researcher at Amnesty International’s Security Lab, calls it double victimization: first you’re hit by one of the most invasive technologies in the world, then you find one dead end after another when you seek justice. Courts and bodies like the European Court of Human Rights take years and cost a lot, and the search wears people down psychologically.

Europe’s own recommendations haven’t helped. After the Pegasus scandal, the European Parliament’s PEGA inquiry committee adopted recommendations on June 15, 2023, including an EU fund for victims’ legal costs and an independent laboratory offering free legal and technical help and forensic analysis. Member states were asked to strengthen safeguards, notify people who were surveilled, guarantee effective remedies and let independent bodies access the data needed to investigate abuses. Three years later, Green MEP Saskia Bricmont says nothing has been done by the Commission or the member states, and that governments hide behind national security.

Sophie in ‘t Veld, the former PEGA rapporteur, says the situation has become worse. She argues that governments realised they would face no consequences and that more spyware cases have emerged since the inquiry, especially in Italy. She also criticises the European Commission for supporting national governments instead of protecting victims. Polish MEP Krzysztof Brejza says the system does not help victims because there is little transparency and no clear process for seeking justice.

Brejza was also a victim of spyware. His phone was infected with Pegasus while he was leading the election campaign against Poland’s then-ruling Law and Justice party. He says attackers accessed 85,000 messages covering ten years and changed some conversations.

“They gained access to 85,000 messages, covering the last ten years of my private and professional life. Because they found nothing against me, they went further and manipulated my conversations. Altered exchanges were broadcast by national television to discredit me. The aim was to interfere in the election by weakening democracy,” Brejza tells IrpiMedia.

National television later broadcast these messages to damage his reputation. Poland’s Central Anti-Corruption Bureau had requested the surveillance as part of an investigation into his father, a mayor. Prosecutors in Gdansk later found no grounds for that investigation.

In October 2026, a Polish parliamentary inquiry concluded that Pegasus had been purchased unlawfully and used against political opponents. So far, Brejza has won only civil cases: the broadcaster was forced to apologise and pay damages. Criminal investigations are still ongoing and progressing slowly.

“In October 2026, a parliamentary inquiry committee set up in Poland after Donald Tusk took office to investigate the use of Pegasus under the previous government concluded that the spyware had been purchased unlawfully and used against political opponents.” states the report.

Poland’s justice minister also serves as prosecutor general, while the former justice minister received asylum in Hungary before moving to the US.

Koukakis says they identified the Predator spyware and its operator but not who ordered the attacks. Court records show that nearly one-third of those targeted in 2020 and 2021 were also under Greek intelligence surveillance. He suspects a link. Fake appointment messages and article invitations were used to lure victims. He believes his reporting on legal changes that allegedly benefited people involved in financial crimes may have made him a target.

Greek authorities deny using Predator, arguing that no law regulated it at the time. Although an Athens court referred the case for further investigation, the Supreme Court prosecutor refused to reopen it on April 27. Koukakis challenged the decision and took his case against Greece to the European Court of Human Rights.

In Hungary, investigative journalist Szabolcs Panyi, who has covered Russian influence on the government of Viktor Orbán, learned from analyses by Amnesty’s Security Lab and Citizen Lab that he’d been spied on with Pegasus for seven months in 2019, with about 100 megabytes of data moving to and from his phone. All he’s found out since is that the civilian intelligence agency holds classified information about him, and every request has been blocked on national security grounds. He says Hungarian law lets anyone be spied on legally, because the justice minister, a member of the government, authorizes it.

Despite Spain’s stricter laws, spyware infected the phones of at least 65 people linked to the Catalan independence movement, mostly between 2017 and 2020, according to Citizen Lab. The victims included four members of Òmnium Cultural. The legal case was dismissed and later reopened on appeal, while the government was asked to declassify related documents.

In 2022, Spain’s ombudsman confirmed that intelligence services had legally monitored 18 independence movement members. However, Òmnium’s Elena Jiménez argues that judicial approval doesn’t automatically make surveillance lawful, warning that even progressive governments can spy on political opponents.

In Italy, Mediterranea Saving Humans founders Luca Casarini and Beppe Caccia, along with activist David Yambio, were targeted with Paragon’s Graphite spyware. The government cited suspected facilitation of irregular immigration, while Casarini believes the real motive was their evidence of abuses against migrants in Libya and Tunisia. Italy’s parliamentary oversight body ruled all three cases lawful.

Citizen Lab founder Ron Deibert warns that spyware creates a worldwide pattern of abuse, silencing victims and weakening democratic accountability. Experts argue that Europe still lacks effective safeguards and oversight. They call for greater transparency and a way to identify who orders and conducts surveillance. As Sophie in ‘t Veld puts it, “It is clear that they feel safe, untouchable.”

“Spyware can be useful in addressing real threats, such as terrorism or crime. But we need tools that allow us to identify the end user of the product, so that, when necessary, we can trace who ordered the surveillance and who carried it out, even in real time,” the journalist Koukakis told IrpiMedia.

Rebecca White, a researcher at Amnesty International’s Security Lab, calls it double victimization: first you’re hit by one of the most invasive technologies in the world, then you find one dead end after another when you seek justice. Courts and bodies like the European Court of Human Rights take years and cost a lot, and the search wears people down psychologically.

Europe’s own recommendations haven’t helped. After the Pegasus scandal, the European Parliament’s PEGA inquiry committee adopted recommendations on June 15, 2023, including an EU fund for victims’ legal costs and an independent laboratory offering free legal and technical help and forensic analysis. Member states were asked to strengthen safeguards, notify people who were surveilled, guarantee effective remedies and let independent bodies access the data needed to investigate abuses. Three years later, Green MEP Saskia Bricmont says nothing has been done by the Commission or the member states, and that governments hide behind national security.

Sophie in ‘t Veld, the former PEGA rapporteur, says the situation has become worse. She argues that governments realised they would face no consequences and that more spyware cases have emerged since the inquiry, especially in Italy. She also criticises the European Commission for supporting national governments instead of protecting victims. Polish MEP Krzysztof Brejza says the system does not help victims because there is little transparency and no clear process for seeking justice.

Brejza was also a victim of spyware. His phone was infected with Pegasus while he was leading the election campaign against Poland’s then-ruling Law and Justice party. He says attackers accessed 85,000 messages covering ten years and changed some conversations.

“They gained access to 85,000 messages, covering the last ten years of my private and professional life. Because they found nothing against me, they went further and manipulated my conversations. In October 2026, a Polish parliamentary inquiry concluded that Pegasus had been purchased unlawfully and used against political opponents. “In October 2026, a parliamentary inquiry committee set up in Poland after Donald Tusk took office to investigate the use of Pegasus under the previous government concluded that the spyware had been purchased unlawfully and used against political opponents.” states the report.

Poland’s justice minister also serves as prosecutor general, while the former justice minister received asylum in Hungary before moving to the US.

Court records show that nearly one-third of those targeted in 2020 and 2021 were also under Greek intelligence surveillance. He suspects a link. He believes his reporting on legal changes that allegedly benefited people involved in financial crimes may have made him a target.

Despite Spain’s stricter laws, spyware infected the phones of at least 65 people linked to the Catalan independence movement, mostly between 2017 and 2020, according to Citizen Lab. Italy’s parliamentary oversight body ruled all three cases lawful.

Experts argue that Europe still lacks effective safeguards and oversight. They call for greater transparency and a way to identify who orders and conducts surveillance. As Sophie in ‘t Veld puts it, “It is clear that they feel safe, untouchable.”

“Spyware can be useful in addressing real threats, such as terrorism or crime. But we need tools that allow us to identify the end user of the product, so that, when necessary, we can trace who ordered the surveillance and who carried it out, even in real time,” the journalist Koukakis told IrpiMedia.

item.title: Microsoft Cloud Outage Hits Outlook, Teams, Copilot and AI Services
item.description:
A Microsoft outage disrupted Outlook, Teams and Copilot, also breaking OpenAI and Anthropic connectors to Microsoft 365 accounts.

Microsoft 365, Outlook and Teams went down for thousands of US users on Thursday, November 12. Reuters reported that the disruption also hit the connectors OpenAI’s and Anthropic’s AI services use to reach Microsoft accounts.

“Microsoft 365, Outlook and Teams were down for thousands of US users on Thursday, ​according to outage-tracking website Downdetector.com, with the disruption ‌also hitting connectors used by OpenAI’s and Anthropic’s AI services.” Reuters states

Downdetector, which collates status reports from several sources, logged more than 97,000 Outlook incidents at 2:07 p.m. ET. It also recorded more than 38,000 reports of Microsoft 365 problems and about 4,500 for Teams. Reuters notes the number of affected users may vary. Expers observed complaints surge that afternoon across Outlook, Microsoft 365, Teams, Copilot, Azure, OneDrive and the Microsoft Store.

In a Microsoft 365 admin center notice (MO1550821), Microsoft warned that users might have trouble accessing several services, including Exchange Online, Teams, SharePoint Online, Microsoft 365 Copilot and Microsoft Defender XDR.

Microsoft said the outage started at 1:26 p.m. ET. However, it had already been investigating problems connecting to Exchange Online mailboxes in the Americas earlier that day. The company later confirmed that users worldwide could be affected.

Microsoft initially blamed heavy workloads across several regions. However, it later found that increased traffic was not the cause. In an update on X, the company said it was working to safely bring several unavailable servers back online. Their loss was putting extra pressure on the remaining infrastructure.

Its response so far has been to pause all deployments, redistribute connection traffic across its worldwide infrastructure and move additional traffic away from affected systems. It’s also restarting the affected servers to restore capacity. In a statement to Reuters, Microsoft said it was aggressively pursuing all pathways to reduce impact.

“We’re aggressively pursuing all pathways to reduce impact,” ​states Microsoft.

“We determined the elevated load isn’t driven by an increase in traffic, but by a number of servers being unexpectedly unavailable; straining the remaining infrastructure. We’re working to safely return them to service,” Microsoft wrote on X.


Microsoft first blamed the disruption on high infrastructure demand across several regions. However, it later found that the issue was caused by servers unexpectedly going offline.

Microsoft also reported a separate Teams outage (TM1550488) that affected users in North and South America from 9:45 to 10:53 a.m. ET. Users experienced delays or failures when sending messages, creating or updating conversations, and retrieving chat messages. Microsoft traced the problem to resource contention within its infrastructure, which increased resource usage and prevented Teams from processing messages properly. The company confirmed that the issue has been resolved.

At this time the massive outage has yet to be resolved. Reuters says Microsoft later told customers the issue may also affect Microsoft 365 connectivity for users in other regions.

The impact also extended to AI services. OpenAI reported problems with its Microsoft connectors, saying new connections might fail and tools might not work properly. Anthropic also reported an issue with its Microsoft 365 connector caused by a problem at an upstream provider. As a result, Copilot and competing AI services were unable to access users’ inboxes because the underlying Microsoft services were unavailable.


IT teams should check the Microsoft 365 admin center for updates rather than make assumptions about the cause. They should also expect emails and messages to be delayed until services fully recover.

Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon

Pierluigi Paganini

(SecurityAffairs – hacking, Microsoft)

item.title: The School Bomb Threats Came From Accounts Already in Stolen Data
item.description:
Hudson Rock researchers found that two university addresses tied to Italy’s school bomb threats were in infostealer data.

On 11 November, bomb-threat emails hit schools across Europe. ANSA, citing the Education Ministry, reported that about 6,000 Italian schools received them. Some evacuated, others kept teaching after talking to police, so the recipient count tells you nothing about how many buildings emptied.

The emails were signed “Mikhail Andropov” and threatened pupils and school staff. They also mentioned a bomb targeting the prime minister. However, these names and claims came from the sender and do not confirm who was behind the threats. Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said that searches found no bombs. She described the emails as an attempt to spread fear and chaos, adding that anonymous messages would not change the school calendar.

The same threats were reported outside Italy. Police in Northern Ireland said that more than 300 schools had received the same message, while Police Scotland classified the cases it investigated as hoaxes. In Ireland, The Journal reported threats against schools and newsrooms sent from different email addresses. This means there is no reason to assume that all the messages came from the same person or group.

Hudson Rock now reports that two university addresses tied to the threats appear in its stolen-credential data.

“The bomb-threat emails that disrupted Italian schools on November 11 have a significant credential-exposure connection.” reads the report. “Hudson Rock identified records for both university email addresses highlighted in threat-related material: [email protected] and [email protected].”

One belongs to an Egyptian university, the other to a Taiwanese one. The company says only that the credentials were exposed. It doesn’t claim they sent the emails, and it doesn’t blame any person, group or state.

The Egyptian address shows up in a Vidar infostealer record from 1 October 2021, taken from a Windows 7 machine running Chrome. The export holds 112 saved credentials, 20 of them using the university address, and two of those point to Microsoft sign-in pages. The same password habits spill across services, so one infected computer exposed a lot more than one account.

That record is more than five years old, which proves exposure and little else. It doesn’t show continuous access, an unchanged password or an infection nobody cleaned. The address also appeared in a newspaper photo and a public post, and the legitimate account holder shouldn’t be treated as the author of the threats.

“The saved credentials also show password reuse across services. That broadens the consequences of a single device infection: the same stolen collection can expose several accounts, including a university identity used on unrelated websites.” continues the report. “The age of the record is an important part of the finding. It places documented exposure more than five years before these threats. It does not demonstrate five years of continuous attacker access, an unchanged password, or an unremediated infection.”

The Taiwanese address turned up in AlienTXTBASE, a collection of aggregated infostealer data that Troy Hunt added to Have I Been Pwned in February 2025. Hudson Rock dates the record to more than a year before the threats. An Italian school published the address after receiving the email, and Focus Taiwan reports that Da-Yeh University found an alumnus account sending a large volume of mail, appearing compromised, and suspended it.

An infostealer copies what a device holds: saved passwords, session cookies, tokens, system details and sometimes wallet data. A stolen password may still open an account later, and stolen session tokens can skip MFA. Nothing in the files shows token theft in either case.

There is still no proof that the stolen credentials were used to send the emails. Full email headers, provider message logs and sign-in records would help identify which account or session sent them. Even if an email passes authentication checks, this does not prove that a specific stolen password was used.

Hudson Rock also discusses what Microsoft and the universities could have done to prevent the abuse. Entra ID Protection can compare leaked credentials with password hashes in an organization’s tenant and apply security policies based on risk. However, this requires an Entra ID P2 or Entra Suite license and proper configuration. The report does not explain what Microsoft or the universities knew about the exposed passwords or whether they were still valid.

A proper response must address the compromised account, its active sessions and the affected device. Organizations should block the account, reset its password through a trusted process and check whether the same password was used elsewhere. They should also revoke active sessions and refresh tokens, review app passwords, unauthorized sign-in methods, application permissions and mailbox rules.

The affected device must also be checked and cleaned. Otherwise, malware on the machine could steal the new password as well. Organizations should also introduce phishing-resistant authentication and monitor sign-in activity and outgoing emails. A sudden increase in outgoing messages should always raise a security alert.

A password reset alone isn’t enough, because some applications control their own sessions and token revocation takes time. An outbound filter won’t stop every first message either. Nobody should need a bomb threat to notice a password has been on the market for a year.

“The disruption illustrates why credential exposure deserves attention beyond fraud and data theft.” concludes the report. “An account associated with an ordinary university user can become a means of reaching schools, frightening families, and consuming emergency resources”

(SecurityAffairs – hacking, school bomb threats)
